newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Two Americans, Briton won Nobel for carbon discovery.
newsitem.headline: Two Americans, Briton won Nobel for carbon discovery.

text.p: Americans Robert Curl and Richard Smalley and Briton Sir Harold Kroto won the 1996 Nobel Chemistry Prize for a discovery that promises to be momentous when it is fully understood, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Wednesday.
The academy said the $1.12 million prize was awarded for their discovery in 1985 of fullerenes, new soccer-ball shaped forms of the element carbon in which the atoms are arranged in closed shells.

Curl, born in 1933 in Alice, Texas, has been a professor at Rice University in Houston, since 1967. Smalley, born in 1943 in Akron, Ohio, is a professor of chemistry and physics at the same university.
Kroto, born in 1939 in Wisbech, eastern England, is a professor of chemistry at the University of Sussex, in the southern English town of Brighton.
Kroto said he was "totally overwhelmed" by the news.
"This is the greatest day of my life. It's fantastic. I'm about to have my first glass of champagne," he told Reuters by telephone from his office in the University of Sussex.
Professor Carl-Olof Jacobson, permanent secretary of the Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, said it was very rare for a scientific Nobel prize to be awarded such a short time after the invention.
"This is such a big discovery that it was awarded with a Nobel Prize after only a few years. This makes it more difficult to say already now what it can be used for," Jacobsen said.
The three men discovered the fullerenes over an 11-day period in 1985 and the discovery has given birth to a new form of chemistry.
"The element carbon has thus assumed an almost infinite number of different structures," the academy said.

The structure, shaped like a soccer ball, was called the "Buckminsterfullerene" after U.S. architect R. Buckminster Fuller, for his design of the geodesic dome at the site of Expo 67, the world fair in 1967 in Montreal, Canada. The shape of the faceted dome closely resembles the chemical structure.
